blocks.body:
For a fixed modulus $q$, the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions says the primes are shared out evenly among the $\varphi(q)$ residue classes $a \bmod q$ with $\gcd(a,q)=1$. Many problems, sieve problems above all, need more than that. They need the even distribution to hold for a huge range of moduli at once, typically every $q$ up to a power of $x$. For one modulus at a time, the best unconditional result, the [[siegel-walfisz|Siegel–Walfisz theorem]], only reaches $q \le (\log x)^A$.

The Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem says that if a statement on average over $q$ is enough, you can go all the way to $q$ of size about $x^{1/2}$. The generalised Riemann hypothesis would give that range for each modulus separately. That is why the theorem is often described as GRH on average. Enrico Bombieri and A. I. Vinogradov proved it independently in 1965.

blocks.title: Measuring the error
blocks.body:
Primes are weighted by the von Mangoldt function $\Lambda$, because that makes the analysis cleanest. Put
$$\psi(x;q,a) = \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ n \equiv a \pmod q}} \Lambda(n), \qquad E(x;q) = \max_{(a,q)=1} \Bigl|\psi(x;q,a) - \frac{x}{\varphi(q)}\Bigr|.$$
The expected value of $\psi(x;q,a)$ is $x/\varphi(q)$: total weight about $x$ (the prime number theorem), shared among $\varphi(q)$ classes. The few prime powers $p^k$ with $p \mid q$ live in the classes with $\gcd(a,q)>1$ and are negligible.

How large can $E(x;q)$ be with no work at all? Each $n \le x$ contributes at most $\log x$, and a class mod $q$ has at most $x/q+1$ members up to $x$, so $\psi(x;q,a) \le (x/q+1)\log x$. Hence $E(x;q) \ll x\log x/\varphi(q)$ for $q \le x$. Since $\sum_{q \le Q} 1/\varphi(q) \ll \log Q$, the trivial bound is
$$\sum_{q \le Q} E(x;q) \ll x (\log x)^2.$$
To say anything useful, a theorem has to beat this by more than a fixed power of $\log x$. That is what Bombieri–Vinogradov does: it saves an arbitrary power of $\log x$ for $Q$ almost as large as $\sqrt x$.

blocks.title: Level of distribution
blocks.body:
The primes have level of distribution $\theta$ if for every $A>0$ and every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\sum_{q \le x^{\theta-\varepsilon}} E(x;q) \ll_{A,\varepsilon} \frac{x}{(\log x)^A}.$$
So $\theta$ measures how far, as a power of $x$, the moduli can go while equidistribution still holds on average.

blocks.title: Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem
blocks.body:
For every $A>0$ there is $B = B(A)>0$ such that, with $Q = x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-B}$,
$$\sum_{q \le Q}\ \max_{y \le x}\ \max_{(a,q)=1} \Bigl|\psi(y;q,a) - \frac{y}{\varphi(q)}\Bigr| \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A}.$$
Dropping the maximum over $y$ gives the catalog statement
$$\sum_{q \le Q}\ \max_{(a,q)=1} \Bigl|\psi(x;q,a) - \frac{x}{\varphi(q)}\Bigr| \ll_A \frac{x}{(\log x)^A}.$$
In particular the primes have level of distribution $1/2$. The implied constant is ineffective, because the proof uses the Siegel–Walfisz theorem.

blocks.title: Step one: characters, and only primitive ones
blocks.body:
The full proof takes a chapter. We give its structure, prove the one inequality that drives it, and say plainly where details are left out.

By orthogonality of [[dirichlet-characters|Dirichlet characters]], for $\gcd(a,q)=1$,
$$\psi(y;q,a) = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi \bmod q} \overline{\chi}(a)\, \psi(y,\chi), \qquad \psi(y,\chi) = \sum_{n \le y} \chi(n)\Lambda(n).$$
The principal character gives $\psi(y,\chi_0)/\varphi(q)$, which is $y/\varphi(q)$ up to the prime number theorem error and an error of $O((\log qy)^2)$ from prime powers sharing a factor with $q$. The rest is at most $\frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi \ne \chi_0} |\psi(y,\chi)|$.

Every character $\chi$ mod $q$ is induced by a unique primitive character $\chi^*$ mod some $r \mid q$, and $\psi(y,\chi)$ differs from $\psi(y,\chi^*)$ only at prime powers dividing $q$, by $O((\log qy)^2)$. A primitive $\chi^*$ mod $r$ induces one character mod each multiple $q = rk$. Since $\varphi(rk) \ge \varphi(r)\varphi(k)$ and $\sum_{k \le Q} 1/\varphi(k) \ll \log Q$, grouping the moduli this way costs only one factor of $\log x$. After the small error terms are taken out, the theorem follows from
$$\sum_{1 < r \le Q} \frac{1}{\varphi(r)} \sum_{\chi \bmod r}^{*} \max_{y \le x} |\psi(y,\chi)| \ll \frac{x}{(\log x)^{A+1}}, \qquad (\ast)$$
where $\sum^*$ runs over primitive characters only.

blocks.title: Step two: small moduli and large moduli
blocks.body:
Small moduli, $r \le (\log x)^C$: here Siegel–Walfisz gives $\psi(y,\chi) \ll x\exp(-c\sqrt{\log x})$ for each non-principal $\chi$. There are at most $(\log x)^{2C}$ pairs $(r,\chi)$, so their total is far below the target.

Large moduli: split $r$ into dyadic ranges $R < r \le 2R$, where $1/\varphi(r) \le (r/\varphi(r))/R$. Then break $\Lambda$ up with a combinatorial identity (Vaughan's identity is the usual choice). It writes $\psi(y,\chi)$ as a few type I sums $\sum_{m \le U} a_m \sum_{n \le y/m} \chi(mn)$, where the inner variable is smooth and long, and type II sums $\sum\sum a_m b_n \chi(mn)$, where both $m$ and $n$ are longer than $U$. Here $U$ is a parameter, and the coefficients are bounded by divisor functions and logarithms.

The condition $mn \le y$ ties the two variables together. A standard Fourier device (a truncated Perron formula) separates them at the cost of a power of $\log x$. With $m$ running over $M$ consecutive integers, $n$ over $N$ consecutive integers and $MN \asymp x$, the bilinear inequality below bounds the type II part of $(\ast)$ in the range $r \sim R$ by
$$\frac{(\log x)^c}{R}\,(M+R^2)^{1/2}(N+R^2)^{1/2}(MN)^{1/2} \ll (\log x)^c\Bigl(\frac{x}{R} + x^{1/2}(M^{1/2}+N^{1/2}) + R\,x^{1/2}\Bigr).$$
The first term is small because $R > (\log x)^C$. The middle term is small because both variables are longer than $U$, so each is shorter than $x/U$. The last term is small exactly when $R \le x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-B}$. That term comes from the $Q^2$ in the large sieve, and it is the whole reason for the exponent $1/2$. The type I sums are handled in a similar way, and $U$ is chosen to balance the two kinds of sum. We omit that bookkeeping.

blocks.title: Bilinear large sieve for characters
blocks.body:
Let $(a_m)$ be supported on $M$ consecutive integers and $(b_n)$ on $N$ consecutive integers. Then
$$\sum_{q \le Q} \frac{q}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi \bmod q}^{*} \Bigl|\sum_m \sum_n a_m b_n \chi(mn)\Bigr| \le (M+Q^2)^{1/2}(N+Q^2)^{1/2}\, \|a\|_2\, \|b\|_2 .$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
We use the multiplicative [[large-sieve|large sieve inequality]]: for $(c_n)$ supported on $N$ consecutive integers,
$$\sum_{q \le Q} \frac{q}{\varphi(q)} \sum_{\chi \bmod q}^{*} \Bigl|\sum_n c_n\chi(n)\Bigr|^2 \le (N+Q^2)\sum_n |c_n|^2 .$$
Since $\chi$ is completely multiplicative, $\chi(mn) = \chi(m)\chi(n)$, so the double sum factors as $A(\chi)B(\chi)$ with $A(\chi) = \sum_m a_m\chi(m)$ and $B(\chi) = \sum_n b_n \chi(n)$. Write $w_q = q/\varphi(q)$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality over all pairs $(q,\chi)$,
$$\sum_{q,\chi} w_q |A(\chi)||B(\chi)| \le \Bigl(\sum_{q,\chi} w_q |A(\chi)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{q,\chi} w_q |B(\chi)|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
Applying the large sieve to each factor gives $(M+Q^2)^{1/2}\|a\|_2 \cdot (N+Q^2)^{1/2}\|b\|_2$. $\square$

The point is that a bilinear sum over many characters can be bounded nontrivially even though nothing is known about any single character. The rest of the proof exists to put $\Lambda$ into this bilinear shape.

blocks.title: GRH on average
blocks.body: GRH on average. Assume the generalised Riemann hypothesis in the following form. For every $q \le x$, every non-principal $\chi \bmod q$ and $2 \le y \le x$, $|\psi(y,\chi)| \le C y^{1/2}(\log qy)^2$, and $|\psi(y)-y| \le C y^{1/2}(\log y)^2$. Show that $\sum_{q \le Q} E(x;q) \ll x(\log x)^{2-B}$ for $Q = x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-B}$.
blocks.solution:
Use the character expansion:
$$\psi(x;q,a) - \frac{x}{\varphi(q)} = \frac{1}{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi \ne \chi_0}\overline{\chi}(a)\psi(x,\chi) + \frac{\psi(x,\chi_0)-x}{\varphi(q)}.$$
The first term is an average of at most $\varphi(q)-1$ terms, each at most $Cx^{1/2}(\log x^2)^2 = 4Cx^{1/2}(\log x)^2$ in absolute value (since $qx \le x^2$), so it is at most $4Cx^{1/2}(\log x)^2$. For the second, $\psi(x,\chi_0)$ differs from $\psi(x)$ by the prime powers $p^k \le x$ with $p \mid q$. Their total weight is at most $\omega(q)\log x \ll (\log x)^2$, so the second term is $O(x^{1/2}(\log x)^2)$. Hence $E(x;q) \ll x^{1/2}(\log x)^2$ uniformly for $q \le x$, and
$$\sum_{q \le Q} E(x;q) \ll Q\, x^{1/2}(\log x)^2 = x(\log x)^{2-B}.$$
Taking $B = A+2$ gives the Bombieri–Vinogradov bound. The difference is that GRH gives the bound for every modulus separately, while Bombieri–Vinogradov gives it only on average, but with no hypothesis.

blocks.title: Errors up to the square root
blocks.body: A numerical look. Take $x = 10^5$ and $Q = 316 \approx \sqrt x$. Compute $\sum_{q \le Q} E(x;q)$ and compare it with the sum of the main terms $\sum_{q\le Q} x/\varphi(q)$.
blocks.solution:
Computing $\psi(10^5;q,a)$ for every $q \le 316$ and every class gives
$$\sum_{q \le 316} E(10^5;q) \approx 0.395\,x, \qquad \sum_{q \le 316}\frac{x}{\varphi(q)} \approx 11.13\,x.$$
So the errors, each taken in the worst class, add up to about $3.5\%$ of the main terms. A numerical experiment at this size cannot test an asymptotic statement with powers of $\log x$ in it, since $\log 10^5 \approx 11.5$. But it shows what the theorem measures. The worst class for each modulus is still close to its fair share when you add up over all moduli up to $\sqrt x$, even though nobody can prove this for any single large modulus.

blocks.title: Exceptional moduli are rare
blocks.body:
Almost all moduli are good. Fix $C>0$. Deduce from the theorem that, with $Q = x^{1/2}(\log x)^{-B(2C)}$, all but $O(Q(\log x)^{-C})$ moduli $q \le Q$ satisfy
$$E(x;q) \le \frac{x}{\varphi(q)(\log x)^{C}}.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the set of $q \le Q$ for which the inequality fails. For $q \in \mathcal{B}$ we have $\varphi(q) \le q \le Q$, so $E(x;q) > x/(Q(\log x)^C)$. Apply the theorem with $A = 2C$:
$$|\mathcal{B}| \cdot \frac{x}{Q(\log x)^C} < \sum_{q \in \mathcal{B}} E(x;q) \le \sum_{q \le Q} E(x;q) \ll \frac{x}{(\log x)^{2C}}.$$
Hence $|\mathcal{B}| \ll Q(\log x)^{-C}$. This is the usual way to read the theorem. The prime number theorem holds in every class with a power-of-log relative error for all moduli up to about $\sqrt x$, apart from a sparse set of exceptions.

blocks.body:
- The theorem says nothing about any particular modulus. A sparse set of bad moduli, for example multiples of a modulus with a Siegel zero, is allowed.
- The maximum over $a$ sits inside the sum over $q$. Averaging over both $q$ and $a$ in mean square is a different, easier statement (the Barban–Davenport–Halberstam theorem), and it reaches $Q$ close to $x$.
- The exponent $1/2$ is a limit of the method (the $Q^2$ term in the large sieve), not a known truth about primes. The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture predicts level $\theta$ for every $\theta<1$. Going beyond $1/2$ is known only in restricted forms, for example for a fixed residue class with well-factorable weights (Bombieri, Friedlander and Iwaniec, 1986) or for smooth moduli (Zhang, 2013).
- The $\pi$ version, with $\mathrm{li}(x)/\varphi(q)$ as the main term, follows from the $\psi$ version by partial summation. Do not mix the two normalisations in one formula.

Bombieri–Vinogradov is the standard input to sieve methods whenever the sequence being sifted is made from primes, such as $\{p+2\}$ or $\{p-1\}$: [[selberg-sieve]], [[sieve-basics]], Chen's theorem towards [[goldbach]], and the Titchmarsh divisor problem $\sum_{p\le x}\tau(p-1)$. It sits on top of [[large-sieve]], [[siegel-walfisz]] and [[l-functions]], and it is the unconditional substitute for [[grh]] in many arguments.

Its most famous use is in [[bounded-gaps]]. Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım showed that any level of distribution $\theta > 1/2$ would give bounded gaps between primes. Zhang (2013) proved a level slightly above $1/2$ for smooth moduli. Maynard's multidimensional sieve works with any positive level of distribution, so Bombieri–Vinogradov is more than enough. The [[twin-primes]] conjecture remains out of reach.

1. Prove the trivial bound $\sum_{q\le Q}E(x;q) \ll x(\log x)^2$ for $Q \le x$, using $\sum_{q \le Q}1/\varphi(q) \ll \log Q$.
2. Show that $\varphi(rk) \ge \varphi(r)\varphi(k)$ for all positive integers $r,k$, with equality when $\gcd(r,k)=1$.
3. Deduce from the theorem a version for $\pi(x;q,a)$ with main term $\mathrm{li}(x)/\varphi(q)$, using partial summation.
4. In the sketch above, identify which term would stop you from taking $Q = x^{1/2}$ exactly, with no logarithmic loss.

sources.ref: E. Bombieri, On the large sieve, Mathematika 12 (1965)
